questions.questionText: After actual performance has been measured and compared with established performance standards, the next step in the controlling process is to take corrective action if necessary.
questions.explanation: The three steps of the controlling process are: 1) Measuring performance, 2) Comparing measured performance to standards, and 3) Taking corrective action[cite: 23]. Therefore, taking corrective action is the logical next step after comparison if performance deviates from standards[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found directly on Slide 8 and Slide 9[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: In order to preserve their position power, managers should avoid doing personal favors for subordinates.
questions.explanation: To increase personal power, a manager should attempt to develop a "sense of obligation toward the manager" among organization members[cite: 23]. Doing personal favors is a common way to build this sense of obligation, thereby increasing personal power, not detracting from position power[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from Slide 16 regarding increasing personal power[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: The process of guiding the activities of organization members in appropriate directions is called controlling.
questions.explanation: Guiding the activities of organization members in appropriate directions is the definition of "Influencing"[cite: 23]. Controlling is defined as "Ensuring that an event occurs as it was planned to occur"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from Slide 4 defining Control, and prior knowledge of the Influencing definition[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Measuring performance is the first step in the controlling process.
questions.explanation: The three steps of the controlling process explicitly list "1. Measuring Performance" as the very first step[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 9[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: For control to be successful, all individuals involved in controlling must have a working knowledge of how the control process operates.
questions.explanation: To make controlling successful, managers must ensure the "Communication of the Mechanics of the Control Process," which means ensuring individuals understand how the process operates[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found on Slide 17 under factors for successful controlling[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Most managers have substantial control over increasing their position power.
questions.explanation: Position power is derived strictly from the organizational position a manager holds[cite: 23]. A manager cannot simply increase this on their own; the organization must promote them. However, a manager can independently work to increase their "Personal Power" by building relationships[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from the definitions of Position Power and Personal Power on Slide 15 and Slide 16[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: In order to preserve their position power, managers should avoid doing personal favors for subordinates.
questions.explanation: Doing personal favors helps develop a sense of obligation, which increases a manager's "Personal Power"[cite: 23]. It does not negatively impact their "Position Power," which is determined by their formal rank in the organization[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from Slide 15 and Slide 16[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Managers identify a problem by comparing the current state of affairs to some standard.
questions.explanation: The controlling process involves comparing measured performance to a standard[cite: 23]. If the performance is "significantly different from standards," the manager must take corrective action, which begins by recognizing the "Problem" (a barrier to goal attainment)[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer derived from the Controlling Process diagram on Slide 8 and definitions on Slide 13[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Controlling does not highlight the deviations in the process.
questions.explanation: The entire purpose of comparing measured performance to standards is to highlight deviations (whether performance is "significantly different from standards") so that corrective action can be taken[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from the Controlling Process diagram on Slide 8[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Corrective actions are necessary after analyzing the deviations.
questions.explanation: If the comparison step shows that performance is "significantly different from standards" (a deviation), the immediate next required step in the controlling process is to "Take corrective action"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found directly on the Controlling Process diagram on Slide 8[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: _________ is managerial activity aimed at bringing organizational performance up to the level of performance standards.
questions.explanation: The lecture slides provide the exact definition: "Corrective action: Managerial activity aimed at bringing organizational performance up to the level of performance standards"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 13[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: _________ is the systematic effort to compare performance to predetermined standards in order to determine whether performance is in line with those standards, or needs to be corrected.
questions.explanation: Roberto Mockler's definition of controlling explicitly states it is "a systematic effort by business management to compare performance to predetermined standards... to determine whether performance is in line with these standards..."[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 6[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an error managers make during the controlling stage of management?

options.content: not taking the time to communicate properly with organization members
not monitoring progress in carrying out plans
not exploring enough viable alternatives for reaching objectives

questions.explanation: Because controlling involves measuring performance to ensure events occur as planned, failing to monitor the progress of those plans is a direct error in the controlling stage[cite: 23]. (Establishing departments is Organizing; communication is Influencing; alternatives are Planning).
questions.reference: Deduced from the definition of Controlling on Slide 4 and general management principles outlined in Chapter 1[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: ________ is the systematic effort to compare performance to predetermined standards in order to determine whether performance is in line with those standards, or needs to be corrected.
questions.explanation: Roberto Mockler explicitly defines 'Controlling' as this exact systematic effort[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 6[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: ________ and ________ have been called the "Siamese twins of management."
questions.explanation: The lecture states explicitly that "Planning and control are virtually inseparable functions, they have been called the Siamese twins of management"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 4[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: The level of activity established to serve as a model for evaluating organizational performance is a(n) ________
questions.explanation: The lecture defines a "Standard" exactly as "The level of activity established to serve as a model for evaluating organizational performance"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 11[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: ________ is managerial activity aimed at bringing organizational performance up to the level of performance standards.
questions.explanation: The lecture defines "Corrective action" exactly as "Managerial activity aimed at bringing organizational performance up to the level of performance standards"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 13[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Because Jamie is the manager, her subordinates follow her instructions. This is an example of ________ power.
questions.explanation: Position power is "power derived from the organizational position a manager holds"[cite: 23]. Since subordinates follow Jamie strictly because she holds the title/position of manager, it is position power[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from the definition of Position Power on Slide 15[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: The level of activity established to serve as a model for evaluating organizational performance is a(n)
questions.explanation: This is the exact, verbatim definition of a "Standard" provided in the lecture[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 11[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: ____ is the management function through which managers compare present performance to preestablished performance standards.
questions.explanation: Controlling is the process that utilizes a systematic effort to compare performance to predetermined standards[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found on Slide 6 under Mockler's definition of controlling[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: As part of the controlling process, you have finished measuring the performance of your team. What must you do next?

options.content: Establish a unit of measure to gauge performance.

questions.explanation: Step 1 of the controlling process is "Measuring Performance"[cite: 23]. Step 2 is explicitly "Comparing Measured Performance To Standards"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found directly on the list of steps on Slide 9[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: This is a fault in the ____ function of management.
questions.context: Gayle has not established appropriate performance standards for her team.
questions.explanation: Establishing performance standards is a core component of the "Comparing Measured Performance To Standards" step within the Controlling process[cite: 23]. Failing to establish these standards prevents successful controlling[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from Slide 11[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of the management by exception concept?

options.content: To focus on minor variances for operational improvements.
To minimize management's involvement in all business operations.
To involve management in every decision regarding business direction.
To notify management only of significant variances from planned results.

questions.explanation: While 'Management by exception' is not explicitly defined in the provided Chapter 21 slides, it is a core controlling concept closely tied to the flowchart on Slide 8: a manager only intervenes (Takes corrective action) when "Performance [is] significantly different from standards"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Deduced from the Controlling Process diagram on Slide 8[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: It is the process of ensuring that events conform to plans.
questions.explanation: The lecture provides the strict definition: "Control: Ensuring that an event occurs as it was planned to occur"[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found verbatim on Slide 4[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: The controlling function is performed by
questions.explanation: Although not explicitly on a single slide in Chapter 21, the controlling process requires that "managers" perform it[cite: 23]. Based on the overarching principles of management (e.g., Chapter 1), all levels of management—top, middle, and lower—execute all four fundamental functions (Planning, Organizing, Influencing, Controlling).
questions.reference: Inferred from the general use of "managers" throughout the slides and fundamental management theory.

questions.questionText: ______ is the management function through which managers compare present performance to preestablished performance standards.
questions.explanation: Controlling is the process of comparing performance to predetermined standards to see if performance aligns[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found on Slide 6 under Mockler's definition[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Controlling function brings the management cycle back to the
questions.explanation: Controlling involves checking performance against plans[cite: 23]. If corrective action is needed, the process flows back to "change plans, organization, or influencing methods"[cite: 23]. Because Planning and Control are "inseparable functions" (Siamese twins), controlling naturally feeds directly back into planning to adjust future standards[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer deduced from Slide 4 and the flowchart on Slide 8[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements does not highlight the relationship between planning and controlling

options.content: Planning and controlling are separable twins of management.
Planning without controlling is meaningless; controlling without planning is blind.
Planning is prescriptive, controlling is evaluative.
Planning and controlling are interrelated and interdependent.

questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly states that planning and control are "virtually inseparable functions" and calls them the "Siamese twins of management"[cite: 23]. Therefore, stating they are "separable" is false and does not highlight their true relationship[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Answer found directly on Slide 4[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Which of the following is not important for controlling function?

options.content: It helps in judging the accuracy of standards.

questions.explanation: Controlling ensures events occur as planned, which promotes coordination[cite: 23]. Therefore, "restricting coordination" is false and not an important or intended outcome of the controlling function[cite: 23].
questions.reference: Deduced from the definition of control on Slide 4[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: Identify the correct sequence of the steps involved in the controlling process.

options.content: Measurement of actual performance, Taking corrective action, Setting performance standards, Comparison of actual performance with standards, Analysing deviations
Comparison of actual performance with standards, Setting performance standards. Measurement of actual performance, Analysing deviations, Taking corrective action
Setting performance standards, Measurement of actual performance, Comparison of actual performance with standards, Analysing deviations, Taking corrective action
Taking corrective action, Measurement of actual performance, Comparison of actual performance with standards, Analysing deviations, Setting performance standards

questions.explanation: Standards must be set first (usually during planning/initial control setup). Then the formal controlling process steps follow: 1. Measuring Performance, 2. Comparing Measured Performance To Standards (which involves analyzing deviations), 3. Taking Corrective Action[cite: 23]. Option 'c' perfectly outlines this logical progression.
questions.reference: Answer deduced from the list of steps on Slide 9 and the definition of a Standard on Slide 11[cite: 23].

questions.questionText: In controlling, reducing the workers, absenteeism in a factory by 20% is an example of
questions.explanation: A standard is a "level of activity established to serve as a model for evaluating organizational performance"[cite: 23]. Because "20%" is a specific, numerical metric, it represents a quantitative standard.
questions.reference: Deduced from the definition of a Standard on Slide 11 and general definitions of quantitative data.
